notes.text: Open — O ye porters, appointed by God for this work. The gates - Of the Lord's tabernacle: where the rule of righteousness was kept and taught, and the sacrifices of righteousness were offered.

The righteous — As David was a type of Christ and the temple of heaven, so this place hath a farther prospect than David, and relates to Christ's ascending into heaven, and opening the gates of that blessed temple, both for himself and for all believers.

The builders — The commonwealth of Israel and the church of God are here and elsewhere compared to a building, wherein, as the people are the stones, so the princes and rulers are the builders. And as these master-builders rejected David, so their successors rejected Christ. Head stone - The chief stone in the whole building, by which the several parts of the building are upheld and firmly united together. Thus David united all the tribes and families of Israel: and thus Christ united Jews and Gentiles together. And therefore this place is justly expounded of Christ, Mark xii, 10 Acts iv, 11 Rom. ix, 32 Eph. ii, 20. And to him the words agree more properly than to David.
Made — Or sanctified as a season never to be forgotten.
We — These seem to be the words of the Levites, to whom he spake ver. 19.

Blessed — We pray that God would bless his person and government. Cometh - To the throne; or from his Father into the world: who is known by the name of him that cometh or was to come, and of whom this very word is used, Gen. xlix, 10 Isaiah xxxv, 4. Name - By commission from him. We - We who are the Lord's ministers attending upon him in his house, and appointed to bless in his name, Num. vi, 23 Deut. x, 8. So these are the words of the priests.

The Lord — Or, The mighty God, as this name of God signifies, and as he shewed himself to be by this, his wonderful work. Who - Who hath scattered our dark clouds, and put us into a state of peace, and safety, and happiness. The horns - These are supposed to be made for this very use, that the beasts should be bound and killed there. These three last verses are David's words. Because this psalm was very large, and the matter of it of the greatest importance, the psalmist thought fit to divide it into two and twenty several parts, according to the number of the Hebrew letters, that he might both prevent tediousness, and fix it in the memory. Each part consists of eight verses. All the verses of the first part beginning with Aleph, all the verses of the second with Beth, and so on. It is observable, that the word of God is here called by the names of law, statutes, precepts or commandments, judgments, ordinances, righteousness, testimonies, way and word. By which variety, he designed to express the nature and perfection of God's word. It is called his word, as revealed by him to us; his way, as prescribed by him for us to walk in; his law, as binding us to obedience; his statutes, as declaring his authority of giving us laws; his precepts as directing our duty; his ordinances, as ordained by him; his righteousness, as exactly agreeable to God's righteous nature and will; his judgments, as proceeding from the great judge of the world, and being his judicial sentence to which all men must submit; and his testimonies, as it contains the witness of God's will, and of man's duty. And there is but one of these one hundred and seventy six verses, in which one or other of these titles is not found. The general scope and design of this psalm is, to magnify the law and make it honourable: to shew the excellency and usefulness of divine Revelation, and recommend it to us, by the psalmist's own example, who speaks by experience of the benefits of it, for which he praises God, and earnestly prays for the continuance of God's grace, to direct and quicken him in his way.

glossa.text:
*Let him now say.* ((ID.)) As I admonish you, so do you admonish one another; or, *let him say,* that is, let him confess.

*Because for ever.* Behold four verses of one ending.

*Open ye.* ((CASS.)) In the third place he desires that the gates of Jerusalem be opened to him, where he speaks also of the corner stone. Open, O prophets, who bear the keys of the kingdom of heaven. *The gates.* ((CASS., HIER.)) They who have entered through these gates of doctrine praise truly; outside the Catholic Church there is no praise of God. ((CASS.)) All these gates lead to one, which is Christ, through whom the just enter into heaven; whence: *I am the door, through which if any man enter in, he shall be safe ((Joan. X))* . And elsewhere: *No man cometh to the Father, but by me ((Joan. XIV))*. ((AUG.)) Behold, he has made mention of both worlds: and because this gate has appeared as Christ, *I will confess to thee,* giving thanks with gladness, *because thou hast heard* at the coming of the Son; for the just of former times were asking for the coming. *The gates of justice.* That is, the gates of death, etc., *as far as* that is, through it unto life.
*They that build.* ((ID.)) The Jews alone, worshipping God, were building, the rest being destroyed through idolatry; but they did not finish, because they despised Christ.
*This is done by the Lord.* Or, *This is done by the Lord for him,* according to another reading. ((ID.)) That is, unto the honour of the Father.

*This is the day.* This is the jubilee year, figuratively observed under the law, which is called *remitting,* or *beginning,* because then bondmen were set free, possessions were restored to their owners: and we on this day have been redeemed from the servitude of sin, to whom an eternal inheritance has been restored. ((CASS.)) *This is the day.* Although he made all days, this one singularly, on which the Lord came, on which it is fitting to rejoice, because the devil lost his right and man lived again; and because this is so,
*O Lord, save,* etc. Behold the desire of a great petition. *Save,* from the ruin of the world. *Give prosperity,* that these sorrows may be turned into eternal joys.

*Blessed,* etc. ((CASS.)) Fourthly he urges that the courts of God be frequented, rejoicing in the coming of Christ. ((AUG.)) Cursed therefore is he that comes in his own name, etc., *as far as* he who shall be cursed. ((CASS.)) *Blessed.* Praise for the coming; and, O ye other Christians, we the elders, as it were priests, *have blessed you,* which profits much, because *we have blessed you out of the house of the Lord.*

*Out of the house.* ((ID.)) That is, the Catholic Church, etc., *as far as* because glad is the confession that follows benefits.

*Appoint a day.* ((AUG.)) The great, who go beyond, who with the mind touch the Word, God with God, etc., *as far as* that is, that he may attain unto eternal joys.

 *A solemn day.* In the old law ((Deut. X.)) the Pasch, Pentecost, the feast of tabernacles, three chief solemnities, in which it was commanded that no man should appear empty in the sight of the Lord. He is empty who has not Christ in himself, who is the foundation, which no man is able to change. Hence it is that on those three solemnities the faithful people offers a coin by an offering of the hand, signifying the inward offering. For on a coin there is the name and image of the king. Let each one therefore offer a coin spiritually, that he may have in himself the *name* of the king, that is, of Christ, being called a Christian from Christ; and may show forth to God the *image,* that is, the soul, marked with the light of his countenance. *The horn of the altar.* ((CASS.)) Or by the *altar* is understood the sacrament of the body and blood, etc., *as far as he shall not have life everlasting.*

Or, the *altar* is understood to be the mind of man; whence in the law it was commanded ((Exod. XXVII)) that an altar be made four-cornered and hollow: four-cornered, because the human mind ought to be fortified with four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance; and the same ought to be hollow to receive the word of God and the fire of love. For swelling drives back what is poured in; whence in Leviticus it is commanded ((Levit. I)) that the little bladder of the throat and the feathers be cast away, when a turtle-dove or a pigeon is offered. The bladder signifies the puffing up of pride; the feathers, empty searchings into lofty things; cast these away therefore, that thou mayest be a hollow altar.

*Thou art my God.* And that we may speak more openly, this is the sense of these words: Let not this feast day upon earth, on which the lamb was slain, suffice: but let it be appointed in frequent celebrations, until with minds exalted we come to his inward Godhead, where we shall sing praises thus: *Thou art my God,* etc. And so, as he began with praise, so he ends with it.
*Give praise to the Lord.* From the beginning which we forsook, unto the end to which we return, there is nothing more wholesome, which may delight, than the praise of God

notes.text: He drew nigh to the place where the borders of Bethphage and Bethany met, which was at the foot of the Mount of Olives. Matt. xxi, 1; Mark xi, 1.
The whole multitude began to praise God — Speaking at once, as it seems, from a Divine impulse, words which most of them did not understand.
Peace in heaven — God being reconciled to man.
Rebuke thy disciples — Paying thee this immoderate honour.

If these should hold their peace, the stones, which lie before you, would cry out — That is, God would raise up some still more unlikely instruments to declare his praise. For the power of God will not return empty.

glossa.text: *And having said these things.* The parable finished, he goes to Jerusalem, to show that the parable had been set forth concerning the fate of that same greatest city, which not long after, being itself also about to kill him for hatred of his kingdom, was to perish by an enemy's slaughter.

*To Bethphage.* Bethphage is a hamlet of priests on the Mount of Olives, and is interpreted *the house of the mouth.* Bethany is a farmstead or city on the side of the same mountain, and is called *the house of obedience.* These the Lord, being about to come to Jerusalem, exalted by his presence, because before his passion he filled many, by teaching, with the gifts of devout confession and of spiritual obedience. Which are well placed on the Mount of Olives, that is, in the Lord himself, who cherishes us with the unction of spiritual chrisms and with the light of conscience and of mercy. And because he does not wish a city set above itself to be hidden, he sends the disciples into the village which is over against them, that through them he may penetrate the fortifications of the whole world set over against him.

*Entering in you shall find.* The preachers, entering into the world, find the people of the nations, entangled in the bonds of unbelief, free and wanton. *Upon whom no man,* etc., that is, no rational teacher has put the bridle of correction, who might either restrain its tongue from evil, or compel it to go into the narrow way of life. No man, by persuading what was useful, bestowed the garments of salvation whereby it might *be warmed.* *No man sat,* because none corrected its folly by pressing it down. *Tied.* Tied with the bonds of unbelief, in which, made over or bound fast, he was serving a lord by error; but he whom not nature but fault had made lord could not claim the mastery for himself. And therefore when the Lord is spoken of, one is acknowledged. For, although there be many gods and lords, yet in general there is one God and one Lord.

*And as they were loosing him,* etc. Despise not this little ass, because as under the clothing of sheep there are ravening wolves, so under the spoils of the body (which is common to us with the beasts) a mind full of God is quickened. *They said.* He had many masters, who, given over not to one superstition, but at the pleasure of unclean spirits, was hurried away to various errors. *Why do you loose him.* Those who had spoken against the loosing of the colt are quiet when the name is heard, because the masters of errors, who withstand the teachers coming for the salvation of the Gentiles, defend their own darkness, until, with miracles bearing witness, the power of the true owner stands forth. But after the power of the Lord's faith appears, the complaints of the adversaries giving way, there is brought forward an assembly that may bear God in its heart.

*The garments.* The garments of the apostles are the teaching of the virtues, or the discernment of the Scriptures, and grace spiritually, wherewith they cover the hearts of men, before naked and cold, that they may deserve to have Christ for their rider. *They laid them on.* While the people of the Gentiles carries Christ, the disciples strew their garments in the way, because, putting off the covering of their own body, they make ready a way for the simple by their own blood, that with unhindered step of mind they may press on to Jerusalem, whither Christ leads, that is, to the true vision of peace.

*At the descent.* As the Lord came down from the Mount of Olives, that is, as he who was in the form of God humbled himself to the weakness of our flesh, the crowds come down with him, that is, he is humbled who need his mercy, that they may be exalted by him. *Rejoicing.* Often he entered the city of Jerusalem, but was not called king, which he had always fled, save only now when he went up to suffer. Which was done for this reason, that he might the more stir up their envy against himself, because the time of the passion was now at hand. *For.* Chiefly for the raising of Lazarus, which had lately been done. For on that account also the crowd came to meet him, because they had heard that this sign had been done by him. They praise him also for the signs and the teaching which he wrought when he went up for the day of the feast of tabernacles, which John relates.

*Blessed.* The crowd, that after a little was to crucify him, calls him king, and declares that the awaited son of David according to the flesh has come, so that a testimony against themselves is wrung from them unwilling. *Peace.* As at the Lord's birth the heavenly companies of men and of angels sang: *Glory to God in the highest. And on earth peace to men,* etc. , so to the same, soon to triumph, men sing together: Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest.

*Master.* Wondrous madness of the envious! Him whom they had known to teach true things, when they hear him called master, they judge that his disciples are to be reproved, as though they themselves were the better taught, those disciples whom he had instructed who by his miracles appears to be God.

*The stones.* When the Lord was crucified and the apostles held their peace for fear, the rocks that were rent, the tombs being opened, openly cried out that he was God and the Lord of the world.

Mystically: if blindness has befallen Israel, so that it falls silent from the praise of God, the people of the Gentiles, their stony heart softened, shall believe and announce their Creator.

praise.title: O Praise Him (All This for a King)

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
echoes.note: The entry on a colt amid royal acclamation enacts Zechariah's oracle of the king coming to Zion humble and riding on a colt, the foal of a donkey. Though Luke does not cite the verse explicitly as Matthew does, the colt and the proclaimed king make this the controlling prophetic background. High volume and coherence with Luke's kingship theme.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The crowd cries 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord,' quoting the pilgrim blessing of Psalm 118:26 with the added royal title 'the King.' This is a direct verbal citation embedded in the Hallel context of festal approach to the temple. High volume; the quotation is explicit and load-bearing.

echoes.text: For the stone will cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the woodwork will answer it.
echoes.note: Jesus's claim that 'the stones would cry out' if the disciples were silent draws on Habakkuk's woe, where the stone cries out from the wall and the beam answers against injustice. The personified crying stone witnessing truth coheres with the inevitability of acclaiming the coming king. High volume; the crying-stone image is rare and distinctive.

echoes.text: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. To him will the obedience of the peoples be. Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Jacob's blessing on Judah foretells the ruler whose scepter does not depart, binding his colt to the vine, an early messianic colt image. The royal colt of the coming ruler coheres with Luke's enthronement entry and the kingly acclamation. Medium because the contact runs through the colt image rather than direct citation.

echoes.text: The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.
echoes.note: Setting the king-to-be on a mount for a processional enthronement recalls Solomon riding David's mule to Gihon to be proclaimed king. The royal mounting and acclamation parallel the Davidic succession ritual, supporting Luke's kingship framing. Medium confidence; the mount differs (colt vs. mule) but the enthronement pattern is strong.

echoes.text: Then they hurried, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs, and blew the trumpet, saying, “Jehu is king.”
echoes.note: Spreading garments before the rider evokes the acclamation of Jehu, where the people put their cloaks under him on the steps and proclaimed 'Jehu is king.' The garment-strewing as royal enthronement gesture closely parallels the crowd's act here. Medium volume; the cloak ritual is a recognizable kingship sign.

echoes.text: Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh from the heavens! Praise him in the heights!
echoes.note: The acclamation 'Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest' echoes the heavenly-praise summons of the Psalms to praise the Lord 'in the heights.' The vertical glory-in-the-highest language coheres with the angelic Gloria pattern Luke reprises. Low because it is diffuse liturgical idiom.

echoes.text: Sing, daughter of Zion! Shout, Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. Yahweh has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, Yahweh, is in your midst. You will not be afraid of evil any more.
echoes.note: The summons to Zion to rejoice because 'the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst' resonates with the rejoicing multitude hailing the coming king at the descent to Jerusalem. The Daughter-of-Zion joy at the king's arrival coheres with Luke's scene. Low confidence; Zechariah 9 is the dominant source.

lines: Throw your cloak in the road, pull the branch from the tree — the King is coming, riding low on a borrowed colt.
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
The whole crowd of disciples is shouting, the road is loud with praise, and even the stones are ready to sing.
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
Open to us the gates of righteousness; this is the day the Lord has made.
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
Hosanna in the highest! Bind the procession with branches and come.
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna!
